title: Progress: which report, which log, which role
blurb: Place any piece of progress information in the right report or log, and match tolerance setting, reporting and escalation to the right management level.
question: On Carrowford's half marathon project, Paceline's race director tells the project manager each week how her work package is going, including a new risk about ambulance cover. Which report is this, and who should receive it?

teach.body: The progress practice has a family of products. Reports move information between levels: checkpoint (team manager to PM), highlight, exception, end stage and end project (PM to board), and the lessons report. Two informal records sit in the project log: the daily log and the lessons log. The digital and data management approach in the PID says how data and information are handled. In plain English: who tells whom, how often, and where the working notes live.

teach.h: The digital and data management approach
teach.body: This PID product, homed in the progress practice, describes how data and information will be created, used and managed across the project ecosystem, through the lifecycle and afterwards, including security and privacy. It supports progress control: stored past performance helps forecasting and automation saves manual consolidation of reports. But data and systems do not set tolerances; the management levels do.

In the build-up stage, Paceline's race director Lisa Ventnor sends project manager Kezia Oduya a weekly checkpoint report, including a new risk about ambulance cover. Kezia sends a fortnightly highlight report to the board. When she forecasts that safety plan approval will slip beyond the stage's time tolerance, she sends an exception report setting out consequences, options and a recommendation. A private chat with the vicar about the churches' letter goes in her daily log; 'consult residents earlier' goes in the lessons log.

rows.label: Timing mats tested; chip supplier late (Paceline to PM)
If approval slips, race day is at risk; three options
Call the vicar on Tuesday about the joint letter
Start road-closure consultation three months earlier

teach.text: Traps: (1) checkpoint reports go from the team manager to the project manager, never straight to the board; (2) highlight reports are time-driven status, exception reports are for a forecast breach; (3) the end project report reviews performance against the PID used to authorize the project; (4) the business layer, not the board, decides on project-level exceptions.

items: Checkpoint: TM to PM. Highlight, exception, end stage, end project: PM to board.
Exception report = forecast breach of stage or project tolerance: consequences, options, recommendation.
Daily log for informal notes, actions and sensitive issues; lessons log for lessons as they arise.
Business layer sets project tolerances; board sets stage tolerances; PM sets WP tolerances.
Digital and data management approach: how data is created, used, secured and kept.

summary: You can now place progress information in the right report or log and recognize each report's sender, receiver and content. You can also match setting tolerances, reporting and deciding on exceptions to the business layer, board, project manager and team manager.

A.q: Carrowford's half marathon project is in its build-up stage. Paceline's race director Lisa Ventnor, who manages the race operations work package, tells project manager Kezia Oduya at the agreed weekly interval that the medical cover subcontract is two weeks late, and that a second ambulance provider may withdraw. In which report should this be recorded?
A.why: A checkpoint report goes from the team manager to the project manager at the frequency set in the work package, including issues and risks for that work package (11.5).

whyNot.0: Highlight reports go from the PM to the board about the stage as a whole.
whyNot.1: Exception reports go from the PM to the board when stage or project tolerance is forecast to be exceeded.
whyNot.3: The end project report is produced in closing to review the whole project.

A.q: Carrowford's project manager Kezia Oduya writes a fortnightly update for the project board: entries stand at 4,100 against 4,500 planned, which is within tolerance; the sponsorship contract is signed; and the churches' letter is being handled. Which report is this?
A.why: A highlight report gives the board a summary of stage status at intervals the board has defined (11.5).

whyNot.1: Checkpoint reports go from a team manager to the PM about a work package.
whyNot.2: Everything is within tolerance, so there is no exception to report.
whyNot.3: The end stage report is produced at the end of the stage to support the next-stage decision.

A.q: Brennan Mutual's Project Skyline is entering its wave migration stage. Stratoshift's delivery lead Arjun Menon, who will manage the wave 2 work package, asks who will set the time and cost tolerances for his work package. Who should set them?
A.why: The project manager sets work package tolerances when authorizing work packages, within the stage tolerances set by the board (11.2.1).

whyNot.0: The executive, with the board, sets stage tolerances, not work package tolerances.
whyNot.1: The business layer sets project tolerances.
whyNot.2: The senior supplier commits supplier resources but does not set work package tolerances.

B.q: Brennan Mutual's executive committee set a project cost tolerance of plus or minus 7.5% for Project Skyline. Project manager Mairi Campbell now forecasts that total project costs will exceed it, and the project board agrees after reviewing her exception report. Who should decide how to respond?
options: The project board, chaired by the executive
The project manager, via an exception plan
Project assurance, for the audit committee
B.why: Project tolerances are set by the business layer, so a forecast breach of project tolerance is decided by the business layer; the board decides on stage-level exceptions (11.2.1, 11.3.1).

whyNot.0: The board decides on breaches of stage tolerance; project tolerance belongs to the business layer.
whyNot.1: The PM may later prepare an exception plan, but does not decide the response to an exception.
whyNot.2: Project assurance gives independent assurance; it does not decide on exceptions.

B.q: Tarnside College's project is near the end of its fit-out and equipment stage. Project manager Leah Whitfield summarizes what the stage achieved, the overall project position and the updated business case, so the board can decide whether to approve the final stage plan. Which report is this?
B.why: The end stage report summarizes progress to date and the overall project situation, giving the board what it needs to decide what to do next (11.5).

whyNot.0: The end project report is produced in closing, not at the end of an intermediate stage.
whyNot.2: Highlight reports give time-driven status during a stage, not the stage-end decision information.
whyNot.3: A lessons report passes on lessons; it does not support the next-stage decision.

B.q: Fernhollow Kitchen is in its development stage. Project manager Nadia Osei makes a note to herself to phone the Dutch line supplier on Monday to confirm the factory shutdown dates. Where should she record this?
B.why: The daily log is the project manager's informal diary for actions, notes, observations and informal issues (11.5).

whyNot.1: The issue register holds formal issues; a reminder to phone a supplier is not one.
whyNot.2: The lessons log holds lessons for this or future projects.
whyNot.3: Checkpoint reports go from a team manager to the PM.

C.q: On Carrowford's half marathon project, Paceline's race director manages the race operations work package. Because Paceline's managing director sits on the project board as senior supplier, she sends her weekly checkpoint reports straight to the board instead of to the project manager. Is this appropriate, and why?
options: Yes, because the senior supplier is on the project board
Yes, because the board needs work package detail
No, because checkpoints go to the project manager
No, because highlight reports are the team manager's job
C.why: Checkpoint reports are from the team manager to the project manager at the frequency set in the work package; the PM reports to the board through highlight reports (11.5, 17.4.2).

whyNot.0: Supplier representation on the board does not change the reporting line from team manager to PM.
whyNot.1: The board manages by exception and receives stage-level summaries, not work package detail.
whyNot.3: Highlight reports are produced by the project manager, not the team manager.

C.q: Calderbrook's Permits Online project is closing. Project manager Hannah Okoro's end project report reviews how the project performed against the version of the PID used to authorize it, and includes a review of the products, the off-specifications and the handover. Is this appropriate, and why?
options: Yes, because the board approved the PID in DP
Yes, because it reviews against the authorizing PID
No, because that review belongs in the lessons report
No, because it covers the final stage, not the project
C.why: The end project report reviews performance against the PID used to authorize the project and includes a product review covering products, off-specifications and handover (11.5).

whyNot.0: The board did approve the PID, but that does not explain what the report should contain.
whyNot.2: The lessons report passes on lessons; the product review is part of the end project report.
whyNot.3: The report reviews the whole project, which is what Hannah's report does.

C.q: During initiation of Wenmoor Community Health's project, project manager Ellie Chandran writes into the digital and data management approach how referral data will be stored, who may see patient-identifiable information, how it will be kept secure and how long it will be kept after the project. Is this appropriate, and why?
options: Yes, because it sets how data is managed and secured
Yes, because all the approaches are part of the PID
No, because data security belongs in the risk register
No, because patient data is the business's concern
C.why: The digital and data management approach describes how data and information will be created, used and managed through the lifecycle and afterwards, including security and privacy (11.5).

whyNot.1: The approaches are in the PID, but that does not explain why this content suits this approach.
whyNot.2: The risk register records specific risks; the rules for handling data belong in the approach.
whyNot.3: The project creates and uses this data, so its handling must be defined for the project.

reteach.title: A school residential trip
reteach.question: A teacher runs a week-long trip with three group leaders. Which messages and notes match which PRINCE2 progress products?

blocks.body: Each group leader texts the trip leader at 6pm with how their group is doing: checkpoint reports. The trip leader emails the head teacher every two days: highlight reports. If the trip will overrun its budget beyond what the head allowed, an urgent message with options goes to the head: an exception report. At the end, a review of the whole trip: the end project report. 'Book the coach earlier' goes in the lessons log; a private note about a homesick pupil goes in the daily log.

head: Trip
PRINCE2
rows: Email to head every two days

blocks.text: Group leaders text the trip leader, not the head teacher: just as checkpoint reports go to the project manager, not the board.

explain.body: An exception report describes the deviation, the consequences if nothing is done, the options and a recommendation. 'What happens if we do not act' is the consequences heading.

test.q: Brennan Mutual's project manager writes in her exception report: 'If nothing is done, wave 3 will finish after the Leeds lease ends, risking member outages and about £400,000 in extra lease costs.' Under which heading of the exception report does this belong?
test.why: The consequences heading sets out what the implications are for the project and the business if the deviation is not addressed (11.5).

whyNot.1: The recommendation says which option is preferred and why.
whyNot.2: The options heading lists the possible ways forward, not the effect of doing nothing.
whyNot.3: A lessons heading would capture what can be learned from the exception, not what happens if nothing is done.

explain.body: The business layer sets project tolerances, the project board sets stage tolerances and the project manager sets work package tolerances.

test.q: Tarnside College's project is about to start its asbestos removal and structural works stage. Who should set the time and cost tolerances for this stage?
test.why: The project board sets stage tolerances and the project manager works within them (11.2.1).

whyNot.0: The business layer sets project tolerances, not tolerances for each stage.
whyNot.1: The project manager sets work package tolerances within the stage tolerances.
whyNot.3: The cost consultant may advise on costs but does not set tolerances.

explain.body: A checkpoint report covers the work package's progress, the products completed, and an update on the issues and risks linked to the work package.

test.q: For Fernhollow Kitchen, Mint and Tallow's account director manages the packaging design work package. At the agreed interval he tells project manager Nadia Osei: 'Sleeve artwork is 80% complete; a new risk is that the recycling logo licence may be delayed.' Which report is this?
test.why: A checkpoint report from the team manager to the PM covers work package status and an update on its issues and risks (11.5).

whyNot.0: The end project report is the PM's review of the whole project in closing.
whyNot.2: Nothing is forecast to breach tolerance, and exception reports go from the PM to the board.
whyNot.3: The end stage report is the PM's report to the board at a stage end.

explain.body: The lessons log is set up in starting up a project and used throughout to record lessons for this project or future ones.

test.q: During the planning and approvals stage of Carrowford's project, project manager Kezia Oduya realizes that the road closure consultation should have started three months earlier. She wants the point captured so that the next event benefits. Where should she record it now?
test.why: The lessons log is the informal repository for lessons that apply to this or future projects, kept throughout (11.5).

whyNot.0: The daily log holds notes, actions and informal issues, not lessons for the future.
whyNot.1: The issue register holds formal issues that need management consideration.
whyNot.2: Highlight reports summarize stage status for the board.
